Wonderful
WUN-der-ful
adj.
Old English wundorfull, full of wonder. Webster 1828: adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing. The modern collapse of the word into a mild compliment is recent; in the Authorized Version wonderful means what exceeds comprehension, and in Isaiah 9:6 it is not a description of the Child but one of His names.

Biblical Definition

Wonderful in Scripture marks the boundary of the creature’s understanding. It is not praise for something pleasant; it names what cannot be taken in. David uses it of God’s knowledge of him: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it (Psalm 139:6). Job, silenced at last, uses the same word of God’s works: things too wonderful for me, which I knew not (Job 42:3). Agur lists what he cannot trace: There be three things which are too wonderful for me (Proverbs 30:18). In every case the word measures a limit, and the man who uses it is confessing that he has reached his. Then Isaiah takes that limit-word and makes it a proper name: his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). The Child born to us is Himself the incomprehensible thing. He is not merely wonderful in His deeds; He bears the name. And the Authorized Version keeps the word in the Gospels for what men saw Him do — the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he did (Matthew 21:15) — where the wonders provoked not worship but displeasure, which is its own commentary on the fallen heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WONDERFUL as adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing; and, as an adverb in older usage, wonderfully. Webster ties it directly to wonder, the emotion excited by novelty or by something that exceeds the power of comprehension.

expand to see more

WONDERFUL, a. — Adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing; as a wonderful prospect. Wonder, n. — That emotion which is excited by novelty, or the presentation to the sight or mind of something new, unusual, strange, great, extraordinary, or not well understood.

Webster’s definition of wonder is the key: not well understood. The word belongs to the limits of the mind. Two centuries of using it for weather and weekends have worn that away, so that a modern reader meets Isaiah 9:6 and hears a compliment where the prophet wrote a name.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 9:6 — "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."

Psalm 139:6 — "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it."

Job 42:3 — "Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not."

Proverbs 30:18 — "There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not:"

Matthew 21:15 — "And when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying in the temple, and saying, Hosanna to the Son of David; they were sore displeased,"

Modern Corruption

Wonderful has been worn down from a word marking the limit of human comprehension into a mild term of approval, so that the titles of Isaiah 9:6 now read as warmth rather than as a claim to deity.

expand to see more

The corruption here is linguistic before it is doctrinal, and it is nearly complete. A word that once meant exceeding the power of comprehension is now spent on meals and holidays. The cost is paid at Isaiah 9:6, where a modern ear hears a string of affectionate epithets for a beloved figure. The prophet is doing something else entirely: he is naming a child The mighty God and The everlasting Father, and Wonderful stands at the head of that list as the confession that the One so named cannot be comprehended by those naming Him. Read as a compliment, the verse becomes sentimental. Read as it stands, it is one of the plainest declarations of the deity of Christ in the Old Testament, and the Christmas card usage quietly disarms it.

There is a second and quieter loss. The three men who use the word of their own limits — David, Job, Agur — are all mature believers, and each is describing something about God he cannot reach. That posture has largely disappeared. A theology that has an answer for everything has ceased to find anything too wonderful for it, and a piety with no room for incomprehensibility will eventually shrink God to the size of its explanations. The Reformed tradition guarded this deliberately with the doctrine of divine incomprehensibility: God is truly known, because He has revealed Himself, and never exhaustively known, because He is God. Job’s confession is not a failure of theology. It is the end of it, and the beginning of worship.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew behind wonderful is a single root meaning to be extraordinary, beyond reach, surpassing. It is the same root that supplies the noun for miracle, which is why the word never means merely pleasant — a wonder is something only God can do.

expand to see more

Hebrew pele (H6382) — a wonder, a marvel, an extraordinary thing; the noun standing as the name in Isaiah 9:6, his name shall be called Wonderful.

The same root gives the verb rendered too wonderful in Psalm 139:6, Job 42:3, and Proverbs 30:18 — literally, too surpassing, out of reach.

In the Old Testament the noun is used almost exclusively of God’s acts; when Isaiah applies it as a personal name, the transfer from deed to Person is the point of the verse.

Greek thaumasios — wonderful, marvellous (Matthew 21:15, the wonderful things that he did). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.

Usage

"Too wonderful for me (Psalm 139:6; Job 42:3; Proverbs 30:18) is a confession of limit, spoken three times by mature men."

"In Isaiah 9:6 Wonderful is a name, not an adjective — the Child is the incomprehensible thing."

"The chief priests saw the wonderful things that he did and were sore displeased (Matthew 21:15); wonders do not produce faith."
